To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Arab culture has a counter productive effect on knowledge sharing attitudes with foreign co workers.
Arab knowledge sharing attitudes differ between different co worker groups.
Arab national culture is counterproductive for knowledge sharing with foreign workers, and that Arab knowledge sharing attitudes vary among different foreign co-worker groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of Arab culture on knowledge sharing and the development of an Arab Knowledge Management (KM) model.
the impact of Arab culture on knowledge management and knowledge sharing in a multicultural workforce.
the Arab national culture's impact on knowledge sharing in the UAE, and the effect of the 'wasta system' on knowledge sharing attitudes in multicultural organisations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Arab knowledge sharing attitudes towards co workers differ according to their national culture, and this difference has a negative effect on knowledge sharing.

the UAE's Arab culture is a major barrier to the success of knowledge sharing in the UAE, and that Arab culture has a counter productive effect on knowledge sharing attitudes with foreign co worker groups, due to heavy emphasis on trust, status, power and social networks and communications, all of these are difficult to achieve within external temporary workers.
the Arab national culture has an adverse impact on knowledge sharing with co workers of other cultures, due to its emphasis on informal communications, strong social networks and 'wasta'.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Arab culture is not homogeneous, but rather consists of a number of different cultural groups, each of which has its own unique characteristics.
Arab national culture, in the UAE, is a significant factor in knowledge sharing attitudes, and that a KM model for the UAE, and other Arab countries, is required.
the Arab KM model is a useful tool for senior management to understand the cultural impact on knowledge sharing and the implications for KM strategy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Arab culture has a negative impact on knowledge sharing with external temporary workers, and Arab knowledge sharing attitudes vary amongst different co worker categories.

a knowledge management model that takes into account the cultural and contextual aspects of a particular organisation and workforce will be more effective and sustainable than a one size fits all approach.
Arab culture can be a double-edged sword for KM.
